title: Inability to Close Doors
hook: The extra option looks harmless until you notice what it keeps stealing from the choice in front of you.
counterintuition: Keeping possibilities alive feels prudent, but every open door charges rent in attention, money, and nerve; wiser judgment names the door that no longer earns its cost and closes it while the decision is still live.
tryThisNow: Pick one option you are keeping warm. Write the next concrete cost of preserving it, then either schedule the real next step or cross it off before the day moves on.
keyTakeaway: Treat open options as active expenses. Close the door that cannot justify its next cost.

breakdown.fastRead: A restaurant team keeps four menu tests alive because each dish might teach them something later. The sensor graph says one test is noisy, one costs too much, and one has lost the dinner crowd. Still, the team keeps all four to avoid regret. That is the inability to close doors: mistaking option keeping for wisdom. An open door is not free just because no one sends an invoice. Name the cost, close the weak door, and give the remaining choice real attention.
breakdown.deepRead:
A half-finished application sits in a browser tab for twelve days. You do not want the job much, but closing the tab feels like killing a future version of yourself. So the tab stays. It asks for small payments: a glance during lunch, a guilty thought at night, a weaker answer to the work already on your desk. The door is still open, but it is not serving you. It is taxing you.

A possible trip, possible hire, possible product line, possible degree, or possible partnership can feel like wealth. Each one seems to expand life. Yet an unchosen option often demands maintenance. You keep checking prices, answering soft emails, holding budget aside, delaying the harder yes. The cost is rarely dramatic enough to force a decision. It leaks out through attention.

Closure buys attention back.

You do not need rash narrowing. Some doors deserve to stay open because new information is coming soon or the upside justifies the carrying cost. The point is to make the cost visible before sentiment makes the decision. Ask what must be paid next to keep this option alive: one more meeting, one more month of rent, one more design round, one more person left waiting. If the next payment would not be worth making on purpose, the door is already asking for too much.

This matters most when the decision has moved from exploration to maintenance. Exploration opens doors to learn. Maintenance keeps them open so you do not have to feel the finality of closing them. The same behavior can look sensible from the outside, but the internal test is different: are you buying information, or buying relief from regret?
breakdown.fullRead:
The museum donor wants all three exhibit concepts preserved until the final gala. The curator nods because every model has a sponsor, a story, and a person who will be disappointed if it disappears. By Friday, the shop has built three partial prototypes, the lighting team has three cue sheets, and the education director has three draft tours that contradict each other. Nothing looks reckless. Everyone can explain why keeping each possibility open is respectful.

That is how this error hides. It rarely sounds like indecision. It sounds like generosity, flexibility, humility, and care for future information. Those motives can be real. The mistake begins when the possibility is treated as free simply because the cost is scattered across people, calendars, storage rooms, and mental bandwidth. A possibility earns its place by beating the cost of keeping it alive.

Dan Ariely's work on keeping doors open made the pressure visible by turning options into literal doors that could disappear. People spent effort preserving doors even when the preserved doors paid less, because losing the door felt worse than following the better payoff. Mark Edmundson's description of students wanting to study, travel, and keep many versions of life available catches the same modern ache from another angle: the open future feels rich, while commitment feels like a theft. The uncomfortable part is that the theft often runs the other way. Too many preserved futures can steal the present decision.

Where are you paying to avoid a small funeral?

The practical move is to separate reversible learning from emotional option keeping. If an option remains open because a specific test will return next week, keep it. Write the test and the date. If it remains open because nobody wants to be the person who closes it, name the carrying cost in public. The cost might be a held budget line, a team split across two designs, a partner left without a firm answer, or a private hour lost to checking a path you no longer intend to take.

The counterargument is fair: closing too early can be stupid. A company can kill a promising product before the market speaks. A student can abandon a course before knowing whether the difficulty is temporary. A city can end a pilot before winter data arrives. The useful test is not decisiveness for its own sake. It asks for a costed door, not a slammed door.

Once the cost is named, closure becomes less theatrical. You can say, 'This option would require two more design days and would delay the main launch by a week.' You can say, 'Keeping this supplier warm means another month without a contract for the team that can deliver.' You can say, 'This application is not research anymore; it is guilt with a login page.' Those sentences change the shape of the choice. The door is no longer a symbol of freedom. It is a line item.

The best closing act is usually small and visible. Remove the option from the menu. Send the no. Archive the draft. Release the budget. Tell the team which version is dead so the living version can get enough oxygen. That is not narrowness. It is stewardship of attention. When a door cannot justify its next cost, closing it is not a loss of possibility. It is the purchase of focus.

examples.title: The menu test with four live specials
examples.scenario: A sensor graph glows above the prep printer in the Toronto restaurant office. Adam must decide between keeping four dinner specials in test or cutting the weakest one before the weekend order goes in. He circles the graph for the smoked trout dish, names the close doors risk in front of the chef, and removes that test from the next order sheet. The kitchen stops splitting prep across a dish customers do not finish.
examples.whatToDo: Mark the live cost of each option, then close the one whose next cost cannot be justified.
examples.whyItMatters: The visible mark turns option keeping from a vague comfort into a concrete operational expense.

examples.title: The case file that waits too long
examples.scenario: "Can we keep both claims alive another week?" the solicitor asks while a cloudy water sample sits beside the legal-aid intake form. Abby has to choose between preserving two weak routes or filing the stronger housing claim today. She labels the sample as option keeping evidence, writes the missed-deadline risk on the triage sheet, and closes the environmental claim until a lab result exists.
examples.whatToDo: Keep a door open only when a named piece of evidence will arrive soon enough to matter.
examples.whyItMatters: A live option can endanger the stronger path when deadlines and staff attention are scarce.

examples.title: The donor exhibit with too many models
examples.scenario: The foam model smells faintly of glue under the museum workroom lamp. Giulia must decide between keeping all three donor concepts alive or retiring one before the fabrication quote. She taps the model card for the glass-walled version, says the possibilities risk out loud, and moves its card to a closed tray while the development director watches.
examples.whatToDo: Use the next fabrication or planning cost as the moment to close a weak possibility.
examples.whyItMatters: Possibilities feel respectful until they force real teams to build around three incompatible futures.

examples.title: The storm shelf with two suppliers
examples.scenario: You are holding queue ticket 41 at the Halifax hardware store service desk while the phone flashes with a second supplier on hold. Steven, the Saturday inventory lead, must decide between keeping both storm orders alive or committing shelf space before the snow warning hits. He writes closure risk on the ticket, cancels the delayed generator order, and gives the receiving clerk one delivery dock instead of two maybes.
examples.whatToDo: Close the option that preserves emotional comfort but blocks a real logistics decision.
examples.whyItMatters: During pressure, open doors can become congestion disguised as preparedness.

examples.title: The churn review that preserves every theory
examples.scenario: It took Aleksy two Friday 4:10 p.m. churn reviews in the Warsaw startup's glass meeting room to see that every theory survived because no one priced the next test. As head of growth, he studies an incident timeline showing three customer exits after a billing change, while the product team still keeps pricing, onboarding, and support theories equally alive. He must decide which path gets a real experiment. He marks the Ariely risk on the timeline and shelves the support theory until new tickets justify it.
examples.whatToDo: Treat each extra theory as a door that must earn the next experiment.
examples.whyItMatters: Ariely's door logic applies when teams spend effort preserving theories that no longer pay.

examples.title: The policy desk with a stale exemption
examples.scenario: What does an old warranty label have to do with a public-comment deadline? Tim finds it stapled to a folder for an appliance exemption that the policy desk has kept open through three review cycles. In the postmortem, he writes inability beside the label, shows the hours lost to preserving the exemption, and closes that route before the next comment packet is assigned.
examples.whatToDo: Use the postmortem to identify which open route survived by habit instead of value.
examples.whyItMatters: Inability to close doors can hide inside administrative continuity, where nobody notices the accumulating cost.

reviewCards.front: An option feels harmless to keep alive. What carrying costs should be counted?
reviewCards.back: Count attention, money, coordination, delayed commitment, and decision drag. An open option is only harmless if those costs are low.

reviewCards.front: A door stays open because new data arrives next week. What is the key distinction?
reviewCards.back: That may be real learning, not avoidance. Keep the door only if the evidence, date, and decision point are named.

reviewCards.front: A team keeps two weak theories alive to avoid regret. What question exposes the bias?
reviewCards.back: Ask what the next experiment or meeting costs, then compare that cost with the value of preserving the theory.

reviewCards.front: Someone says closing a possibility is narrow-minded. What is the reply?
reviewCards.back: Closing is narrow only when the door still earns its cost. Otherwise it is stewardship of attention and commitment.

reviewCards.front: What visible act helps close a door cleanly?
reviewCards.back: Remove the option from the live system: archive the draft, cancel the meeting, release the budget, or tell the waiting person no.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Price open options before preserving them. Keep a door open only when its next cost buys useful information or protection.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a team wants to keep two versions alive, then I will ask for the next cost of each version before approving more work.
If I keep a possible path on my list, then I will schedule a decision date or close it now.
If a backup option delays commitment to a strong option, then I will name the delay risk before preserving the backup.
If a theory survives a review, then I will attach one evidence test and one closure condition to it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one option you are keeping warm. Write the next payment it requires, then send the closing message or define the exact evidence that would keep it alive.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review your open loops and close one door that survives mainly because finality feels unpleasant.

memorableLines.text: An open door is not free just because no one sends an invoice.
A possibility earns its place by beating the cost of keeping it alive.
